_about: The behavioral twin's reviewed recommendation library (twin_recommend.py). Food swaps stay in swaps.json and are offered alongside these. Every item is reviewed:false until the nutrition and behavioral team approves it. Participant-facing text has no digits and passes the chat guardrail (tests/test_twin_library.py). Fields: domains (diet|activity|sleep), type (add|modify|grocery|routine|plan), targets.patterns (twin_patterns keys; one must be confirmed), targets.focus_areas (diet: the participant's focus area must be listed; null = any), targets.general (offered without a confirmed pattern once the domain is in play), contexts (where it happens; 'anywhere' fits everyone), fits (circumstances it suits, the one it was designed around first), helps (constraints it respects), anchor (the existing routine it attaches to, if any), when_options, bct (behavior-change techniques, BCT Taxonomy v1), effort (low|medium), cost (none|low|some), needs (none|microwave|stove), new_time_block (needs time carved out), tags (foods/activities, for allergies, dislikes and 'not for me'), log_categories (diet), grocery (items for the grocery list), coping (if-then plans for likely barriers).

grains_white_rice: Brown rice or quinoa (microwave cups work)

items.title: Fruit with the breakfast you already have
items.text: Add a piece of fruit or a handful of berries to whatever you usually eat in the morning. Nothing else changes.

coping.if: If there's no fresh fruit around
coping.then: a cup of frozen berries or a fruit cup works too

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 and Chapter 4 (fruit); USDA MyPlate, Fruit Group (myplate.gov)

items.title: Fruit in your bag for between classes
items.text: Take a piece of fruit from the dining hall or your kitchen when you leave in the morning, so there's something to reach for between classes.

coping.then: I'll keep it by my keys or in my bag the night before

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (fruit); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (BCT Taxonomy v1: restructuring the physical environment)

items.title: Fruit that keeps, on your grocery list
items.text: Apples, clementines and frozen berries last for days, so fruit is there when you want it.

coping.if: If fresh fruit costs more this week
coping.then: frozen or canned fruit in its own juice counts the same

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (fruit); USDA MyPlate, Fruit Group tips (myplate.gov)

items.title: Vegetables added to a meal you already like
items.text: Ask for extra vegetables, or add a side of greens, to a bowl, pasta or sandwich you already get.

coping.if: If there are no vegetables at that station
coping.then: I'll grab a side salad from the salad bar

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (vegetables); USDA MyPlate, Vegetable Group (myplate.gov)

items.title: Frozen vegetables on your grocery list
items.text: A bag of frozen vegetables keeps for weeks and goes into ramen, rice, pasta or eggs with just a microwave.

coping.if: If the freezer is full or tiny
coping.then: a can of no-salt-added vegetables works too

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (vegetables); USDA MyPlate, Vegetable Group tips (myplate.gov)

items.title: Beans in your burrito or bowl
items.text: When you order a burrito, tacos or a bowl, add black or pinto beans. Same order, one extra spoonful.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (beans, peas and lentils); USDA MyPlate (myplate.gov)

items.title: Low-sodium canned beans on your grocery list
items.text: Canned beans are ready to eat after a rinse. Add them to a salad, rice, a wrap or ramen.
grocery: Low-sodium canned black or pinto beans
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (beans, peas and lentils; sodium); USDA MyPlate (myplate.gov)

items.title: The whole-grain option when you order
items.text: Many sandwich and bowl places offer wheat bread, brown rice or a whole wheat wrap. Ask for it with the order you already like.

coping.then: I'll pick it next time somewhere that has one

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (grains: make half your grains whole grains)

items.title: Whole-grain bread or tortillas on your grocery list
items.text: Next time you buy bread or tortillas, pick the whole wheat kind. Everything you make with them stays the same.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (grains); USDA MyPlate, Grains Group (myplate.gov)

items.title: Yogurt cups or milk on your grocery list
items.text: Yogurt cups, milk or fortified soy milk keep in a mini fridge and make an easy breakfast or snack.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (dairy and fortified soy alternatives); USDA MyPlate, Dairy Group (myplate.gov)

items.title: A handful of nuts or seeds as a snack
items.text: Keep a small bag of unsalted nuts or seeds in your bag or desk for the afternoon.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (protein foods: nuts and seeds; fats)

items.title: Fish or beans when you order out
items.text: When you order out, try a fish taco, a tuna or salmon roll, or a bean option once a week in place of your usual pick.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (seafood; beans, peas and lentils)

items.title: Tuna pouches, peanut butter or canned beans on your list
items.text: These need no kitchen, keep for weeks and add protein to a sandwich, rice or crackers.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (protein foods); USDA MyPlate, Protein Foods Group (myplate.gov)

items.title: Olive or canola oil in the pan
items.text: When you cook and the pan needs fat, use olive or canola oil in place of butter. The rest of the recipe stays the same.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (saturated fat; oils); AHA Life's Essential 8 diet guidance

items.title: Grilled now and then when you order
items.text: When the menu has the same item grilled or fried, pick grilled every so often. Keep the sides you like.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (saturated fat); AHA Life's Essential 8 diet guidance

items.title: Sauce or dressing on the side
items.text: Ask for sauce or dressing on the side and add it yourself, as much as you like.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (sodium, mostly from packaged and restaurant foods)

items.title: Low-sodium versions on your grocery list
items.text: For canned soup, beans and vegetables, pick the low-sodium or no-salt-added can. Season it the way you like at home.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (sodium); FDA, Sodium in Your Diet (fda.gov)

items.title: Flavor from herbs, lemon or pepper
items.text: When you cook, reach for garlic, pepper, lemon or a salt-free seasoning blend first, then taste before adding salt.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (sodium); AHA, sodium and flavor tips (heart.org)

items.title: A water bottle that goes everywhere
items.text: Keep a refillable bottle in your bag, so water is the easy drink between classes and at your desk.

coping.then: I'll fill it at night and put it by the door

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (added sugars; sugar-sweetened beverages); CDC, Get the Facts: Drinking Water (cdc.gov)

items.title: Sparkling water or unsweetened tea on your list
items.text: Have a fizzy or cold drink you like at home that isn't sweetened, for the times you'd usually grab a soda.
items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 1 (added sugars; beverages)

items.title: The long way between two classes
items.text: On class days, take a longer walking route between two of your classes. It fits into time you already spend moving.

coping.if: If it's raining or very hot
coping.then: I'll take an indoor route through a building
I'll take the long way after class instead

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018), 'move more and sit less'; Gardner, Lally & Wardle, Br J Gen Pract 2012 (habit formation)

items.title: A short walk after lunch
items.text: After lunch on weekdays, walk for a little while before you sit back down: around the block, to a farther building, or with a friend.

coping.then: I'll walk the halls or take the stairs instead

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018); Gollwitzer, Am Psychol 1999 (implementation intentions)

items.title: Stairs in a building you use every day
items.text: Pick one building you go to most days and take the stairs there instead of the elevator.
items.anchor: a building you use every day
items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018), 'some physical activity is better than none'

items.title: Move during study breaks
items.text: When you take a study break, stand up and move: a lap of the floor, a few stretches, or a walk to refill your water.

coping.if: If I lose track of time
coping.then: I'll set a timer for my study blocks

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018), 'move more and sit less'

items.title: A short version of your weekend activity on one weekday
items.text: Pick one weekday this week and do a shorter version of what you already enjoy on weekends.

coping.then: I'll move it to the next free afternoon

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (graded tasks)

items.title: Walk or bike one part of your trip
items.text: Walk or bike one part of the trip you already make, like parking a little farther away or getting off the bus a stop early.

coping.then: I'll do the usual trip and take the stairs once I'm there

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018), active transportation

items.title: A walk with a friend or roommate
items.text: Ask a friend or roommate to walk with you once this week, to dinner, to get coffee, or just around campus.
items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (social support)

items.title: Try one class at the campus rec center
items.text: Pick one group class or open session at the rec center that sounds fun and put it in your calendar.
items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018)

items.title: An easy walk on weekend mornings
items.text: Keep weekends restful, and add an easy walk outside one morning if you feel like it.
items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018)

items.title: One wake-up time for class days
items.text: Pick one wake-up time for class days and keep weekend mornings close to it.

coping.then: I'll still get up near my usual time and rest a little in the afternoon

items.source: Watson et al., Sleep 2015 (AASM/SRS adult sleep consensus); Phillips et al., Sci Rep 2017 (irregular sleep in college students); CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep)

items.title: An alarm that means: start winding down
items.text: Set a second evening alarm on class nights that means it's time to start getting ready for bed.

coping.if: If I have a deadline that night
coping.then: I'll start winding down as soon as it's done

items.source: Irish et al., Sleep Med Rev 2015 (sleep hygiene review); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (prompts/cues)

items.title: Charge your phone across the room
items.text: Plug your phone in across the room at night, so it's an alarm and not the last thing you scroll.
items.source: Irish et al., Sleep Med Rev 2015 (sleep hygiene review); CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep)

items.title: A stopping time for studying on class nights
items.text: Pick a time on class nights when studying stops for the day, and plan the next morning's first task before you close the laptop.

coping.then: I'll move the stopping time a little later, not drop it

items.source: Hershner & Chervin, Nat Sci Sleep 2014 (sleepiness among college students); Gollwitzer, Am Psychol 1999 (implementation intentions)

items.title: Outside light soon after you wake up
items.text: Get some daylight soon after you wake up: open the blinds, or walk outside on the way to class.
items.source: Blume, Garbazza & Spitschan, Somnologie 2019 (light and circadian rhythms); CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep)

items.title: Your last coffee or energy drink earlier in the day
items.text: Move your last coffee, tea or energy drink of the day to the early afternoon, so it's worn off by bedtime.
items.source: Drake et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2013 (caffeine taken hours before bedtime); CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep)

items.title: Earplugs, an eye mask or a fan
items.text: In a shared room, earplugs, an eye mask or a fan can make it easier to fall asleep when others are still up.
items.source: Irish et al., Sleep Med Rev 2015 (sleep environment); CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep)

items.title: A lights-out time you agree on with your roommate
items.text: Talk with your roommate about a lights-out time for class nights that works for both of you.
items.source: CDC, Tips for Better Sleep (cdc.gov/sleep); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (social support)

items.title: Weekend bedtimes close to your weekday ones
items.text: On weekends, go to bed and get up within about an hour of your class-day times.

coping.if: If I'm out late on a weekend
coping.then: I'll still get up near my usual time

items.source: Wittmann et al., Chronobiol Int 2006 (social jetlag); Phillips et al., Sci Rep 2017 (sleep regularity in college students)

items.title: Set out tomorrow's breakfast as part of getting ready for bed
items.text: When you start winding down on class nights, put tomorrow's breakfast where you'll see it, so mornings start easier and bedtime has a routine.

coping.then: I'll take something from the dining hall on the way to class

items.source: Gollwitzer, Am Psychol 1999 (implementation intentions); Gardner, Lally & Wardle, Br J Gen Pract 2012 (habit formation); Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4

items.title: A grab-and-go breakfast for class days
items.text: Something you can eat on the walk: a piece of fruit with a yogurt cup, a boiled egg or a nut butter sandwich.

coping.then: I'll grab fruit and a yogurt from the dining hall on the way

items.source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4 (adults); USDA MyPlate, breakfast tips (myplate.gov)

items.title: Walk to breakfast before your first class
items.text: On class days, walk to a dining hall for a quick breakfast on the way to your first class. Movement and breakfast in one trip.
items.anchor: your trip to your first class

coping.then: I'll grab fruit and go, and walk the long way at lunch

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018); Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020–2025, Chapter 4

items.title: Same wake-up time, then breakfast first
items.text: On class days, get up at the same time and make breakfast the first thing you do, even something small.
items.source: Watson et al., Sleep 2015 (AASM/SRS adult sleep consensus); Gardner, Lally & Wardle, Br J Gen Pract 2012 (habit formation)

items.title: An evening walk to start winding down
items.text: After dinner, a short easy walk outside can be the first step of your night routine.

coping.then: I'll walk inside or stretch instead

items.source: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd ed. (HHS, 2018); Irish et al., Sleep Med Rev 2015 (sleep hygiene)

items.title: A minute each night to plan tomorrow
items.text: Before bed, look at tomorrow and pick when you'll eat, when you'll move, and when you'll head to bed. One small plan for the whole day.
items.source: Gollwitzer, Am Psychol 1999 (implementation intentions); Michie et al., Ann Behav Med 2013 (action planning)
